sections.overview: The ruddy turnstone is a stocky, colourful shorebird that takes its name from its habit of flipping over stones and seaweed to find food. It breeds in the Arctic and winters on coasts across much of the world.
sections.identification: A small, robust wader, smaller than a Redshank, weighing roughly 95–125 g with a wing of about 157 mm. It has chestnut and black upperparts, a black-and-white head, white underparts, orange legs and a short, slightly upturned black bill. The sexes look alike.
sections.habitat: It breeds on Arctic tundra and does not nest in Britain. In winter it uses almost any coastal habitat, with a preference for rocky shores, but also sandy beaches and estuaries.
sections.diet: It flips small stones on the tideline to find small crustaceans and insects, and is famously indiscriminate about what it eats. It also takes molluscs, worms and carrion, and can open barnacles and bivalves with its stout bill.
sections.behavior: Turnstones spend much of their time creeping and fluttering over rocks, turning things over as they go. Outside the breeding season they form flocks, often mixed with other shorebirds. Summering birds in Britain are usually young individuals that have not reached breeding condition.
sections.reproduction: A pair typically raises one brood a year, laying four eggs (sometimes three to five). The female mainly incubates them for 22–24 days. The precocial chicks fledge after about 19–21 days. Breeding typically starts at two years of age.
sections.ecology: On the breeding grounds, jaegers, gulls, ravens and foxes take mostly eggs and young; adults are rarely caught, mainly by falcons and owls. The turnstone in turn preys on large numbers of insects on the tundra and of crustaceans and molluscs on the shore.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern, but it is Amber-listed in the UK. About 43,000 turnstones winter in the UK (2012–17); numbers fell by 17% between 1998 and 2023, but the long decline since the mid-1980s has levelled off. Threats include coastal habitat change and disturbance. The oldest ringed bird reached 20 years.
